Electric Charge, Fields & Coulomb's Law

Electrostatics — where charge meets force

22.0 — History of Electromagnetism

The existence of static electricity has been known since antiquity. The Greeks (~500 BC) observed such effects while polishing amber, which would attract bits of straw. In fact, the word “electric” comes from the Greek word “ἤλεκτρον” (elektron) — meaning amber.

As early as the 11th century, a magnetic needle was used for navigation as described by Shen Kuo (1031–1095 AD). About two hundred years later, Petrus Peregrinus de Maricourt used a needle placed on a rounded spherical natural magnet or lodestone to mark longitudinal lines “with two points at opposite ends of the stone through which all the circles passed” on the magnet’s surface. He called these points the poles of the magnet, as the circles resembled the longitudinal lines of the earth along with the north and south poles.

“Struck by the analogy, Peregrinus proposed to call these two points the poles of the magnet: and he observed that the way in which the magnets set themselves and attract each other depends solely on the position of their poles, as if these were the seat of the magnetic power.”

Shortly before the time of Galileo, a man named William Gilbert (1544–1603) published a work on electricity and magnetism, “with which the modern history of both subjects begins,” in which he coined the term “electric force.” Gilbert made the following distinction between electric force and magnetic force:

“The lodestone attracts only magnetizable substances, whereas electrified bodies attract everything. The magnetic attraction between two bodies is not affected by interposing a sheet of paper or a linen cloth, or by immersing the bodies in water, whereas the electric attraction is readily destroyed by screens. Lastly, the magnetic force tends to arrange bodies in definite orientations while the electric force merely tends to heap them together in shapeless clusters.”

Electricity refers to the movement of electric charges and the electric fields produced by charges. Magnetism refers to the magnetic fields produced by moving charges. The term “electricity” was introduced by Sir Thomas Browne.

Although not knowing the fundamental connection between electromagnetism and the phenomenon of light, scientists such as Christiaan Huygens (1629–1695), Robert Hooke (1635–1703), and Isaac Newton (1642–1726) investigated the nature of light.

A little while later, one of the first Americans elected to the Royal Society, Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790), performed experiments with electricity. Most notably, his lightning rod experiment “demonstrated a connection between lightning and static electricity.”

Not long after, an Italian scientist named Luigi Galvani (1737–1798) was experimenting with “animal electricity” and used static electricity from a charged scalpel to contract the leg muscles of dead frogs. Continuing his work, Galvani realized that by joining two pieces of copper and zinc together end-to-end, the same effect of static electricity could be produced.

Alessandro Volta disputed Galvani’s explanation. He suspected the frog was incidental — that the electricity came from the junction of two dissimilar metals, not from the animal at all. To prove it he stacked alternating discs of copper and zinc separated by brine-soaked cloth, removing the frog entirely, and the effect persisted. That stack was the “voltaic pile” — the first battery.

*Worth pausing on: the phenomenon is still called galvanism, and the process of galvanization (coating steel with zinc, first done by Stanislas Sorel in 1836) still bears Galvani’s name — even though Volta was the one who got the physics right. Being wrong about the mechanism while being right that something was there* is how a great deal of science actually proceeds.*

As mankind became capable of intentionally displacing charges with the voltaic pile and moving them with conductors, the connection between electricity and magnetism was inevitable. Hans Ørsted discovered magnetic needles are affected by voltaic current. Michael Faraday developed the modern concept of electric and magnetic fields. Using Faraday’s concept of lines of force, James Clerk Maxwell produced his electromagnetic theory.

Subsequent investigations revealed that atomic and molecular interactions, such as the forces of friction, cohesion, and adhesion, are due to the electromagnetic force. In fact, all forces that we experience on a daily basis, such as the sensation of touch and even the perception of gravity, are the result of the electromagnetic interactions of molecules!

To put things in perspective, here are the relative strengths of the Fundamental Forces, compared between two protons roughly a nuclear diameter apart (\(\sim 10^{-15}\) m):

Force Relative strength (gravity \(\equiv 1\))
Strong Nuclear Force 10³⁸
Electromagnetic Force 10³⁶
Weak Nuclear Force 10²⁵
Gravitational Force 1

*Read that table carefully: “relative strength” is not a property a force simply has. It depends on which particles you compare and how far apart they are — the strong force, in particular, does not fall off with distance the way the other three do, so quoting it without a separation is meaningless. We will meet a different number for the electromagnetic-to-gravitational ratio in §22.2, for exactly this reason.

This chapter begins the study of electromagnetic phenomena at a fundamental level, where charges are at least temporarily stationary — electrostatics.

The next several chapters will be devoted to static electricity, moving charges (current), and magnetism — collectively referred to as electromagnetism.

22.1 — Static Electricity and Charge: Conservation of Charge

As mentioned previously, friction is a result of electromagnetic phenomena, so many characteristics of static electricity can be explored by rubbing materials together, such as walking on carpet, clothes tumbling in the dryer, lightning in the air, or rubbing a balloon in your hair.

Some of the most basic characteristics of Static Electricity include:

  • The effects of static electricity are explained by a physical quantity known as electric charge
  • There are only two types of charge: Positive and Negative (Neutral is the absence of net charge!)
  • Like charges repel whereas opposite charges attract
  • Electric force between charges varies with distance

Given that electric charge is the basis for describing the effects of static electricity, how do we know that there are only two types of charges?

By rubbing various materials together, certain combinations of materials always produce one type of charge on one material and the opposite type of charge on the other material.

For example, glass rubbed with silk causes the glass to become positively charged while the silk becomes negatively charged. Since the materials have opposite charges, they attract. Two glass rods rubbed with silk will repel each other as each rod is positively charged, while two silk cloths rubbed on glass will repel each other as each silk cloth is negatively charged.

With a reasonable convention established, we are led to ask some more sophisticated questions:

  • Where do these charges come from?
  • Can you create or destroy charge?
  • Is there a “smallest” unit of charge?
  • How does force depend on the distance between charges? What about its magnitude?

Origin of Charge: The Atomic Model

So then, where do these charges come from? The atomic model reveals that charge is carried by electrons and protons. A simple model of an atom depicts electrons orbiting a nucleus.

Electrons are negatively charged while protons are positively charged, and neutrons are neutral, with no charge. The nucleus of an atom is positively charged due to the protons bonded with the neutrons.

Nearly all charge in the universe is carried by electrons and protons. Other charge-carrying particles are observed in cosmic rays and nuclear decay and are “created” in particle accelerators/colliders (discovered via conservation of charge and energy).

The charges of electrons and protons are identical in magnitude but opposite in sign. Usually, net charges are formed by combinations of electrons and protons. An electron or a proton has a charge, \(q\), of magnitude:

\[q_e = e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\]

This is the elementary charge — the smallest unit of free charge observed in nature. Charge is quantized, meaning it comes in discrete multiples of this fundamental unit.

The units of charge, Coulombs (C), are named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb (1736–1806).

How Big is a Coulomb?

Okay, but what the heck is a Coulomb of charge? Well, instead let’s ask how many protons or electrons are needed to produce 1 Coulomb of charge!

To determine the number of protons to make 1 Coulomb of positive charge:

\[1.00\ \text{C} \times \left(\frac{1\ \text{proton}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}}\right) = 6.24 \times 10^{18}\ \text{protons}\]

And the number of electrons to make 1 Coulomb of negative charge is equivalent: \(6.24 \times 10^{18}\) electrons.

For comparison’s sake: light travels \(10^{18}\) meters in a century, and the age of the universe is approximately \(10^{18}\) seconds. A Coulomb is a LOT of charge!

Conservation of Charge

Just as we learned that energy and momentum are conserved in Physics I, electric charge is also conserved. The total charge in an isolated system remains constant — charge can be transferred from one object to another, but it cannot be created or destroyed.

This principle was crucial in discovering new particles in particle accelerators: if the charge before a collision doesn’t match the charge after, there must be an undiscovered particle carrying the missing charge!

Conductors and Insulators

Electrical conductors are materials in which some of the electrons are free electrons that are not bound to atoms and can move relatively freely through the material.

Electrical insulators are materials in which all electrons are bound to atoms and cannot move freely through the material.

Semiconductors (like silicon and germanium) have properties between conductors and insulators, and their conductivity can be controlled — the basis of modern electronics.

How Objects Actually Become Charged

Charge is never created — only moved. There are three ways to move it, and they explain every static-electricity effect you have ever seen.

By friction. Rubbing two materials together transfers electrons from one to the other. Which direction they go depends on the pair, not on either material alone — this is why glass-on-silk and rubber-on-fur charge oppositely.

By conduction (contact). Touch a charged object to a neutral conductor and free electrons flow between them until both share the excess. Both objects end up with charge of the same sign.

By induction (no contact). Bring a negative rod near an isolated conductor without touching it. The free electrons in the conductor are repelled to the far side, leaving the near side positive. Ground the far side and those electrons escape entirely; remove the ground, then the rod, and the conductor is left positively charged — the opposite sign to the rod that charged it, and the rod never lost any charge of its own.

Polarization is the insulator’s version. Insulators have no free electrons, so nothing can migrate across the object. Instead each molecule stretches slightly, its electron cloud shifting away from an approaching negative charge. The object stays neutral overall, but its near face is now slightly positive.

That last mechanism answers the question Gilbert raised at the start of this chapter — why “electrified bodies attract everything,” charged or not. A charged rod polarizes a scrap of neutral paper; the induced near-face charge is slightly closer to the rod than the far-face charge, and since the Coulomb force falls off as \(1/r^2\), the attraction wins. Neutral does not mean unaffected.

22.2 — Coulomb’s Law

The Force Between Charges

Having established that charges exist and come in two types, we now ask: How do charges interact? What is the mathematical form of the electric force?

Charles-Augustin de Coulomb (1736–1806) used a torsion balance (similar to Cavendish’s apparatus for measuring gravitational attraction!) to precisely measure the force between charged objects.

Coulomb’s Law gives the magnitude and direction of the electric force between two charged particles:

\[\vec{F} = k_e \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} \hat{r}\]

where:

  • \(k_e\) is Coulomb’s constant
  • \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) are the magnitudes of the charges
  • \(r\) is the distance between the charges
  • \(\hat{r}\) is the unit vector pointing from one charge to the other

The magnitude of the force is:

\[F = k_e \frac{|q_1||q_2|}{r^2}\]

Gravitational Analogy

Compare Coulomb’s Law to Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation:

Gravitational Force Electric Force
\(F_g = G\dfrac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}\) \(F_E = k_e\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\)
\(G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \frac{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}{\text{kg}^2}\) \(k_e = 8.988 \times 10^{9}\ \frac{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}{\text{C}^2}\)
Always attractive Attractive OR repulsive
Source: mass Source: charge

Both are inverse-square laws — the force decreases with the square of the distance. However, there is a crucial difference: gravity is always attractive (masses always attract), while the electric force can be attractive (opposite charges) or repulsive (like charges).

Notice the enormous difference in the constants! This is why the electromagnetic force is so much stronger than gravity at the atomic scale.

Coulomb’s Constant and Permittivity

Coulomb’s constant can also be written in terms of the permittivity of free space, \(\varepsilon_0\):

\[k_e = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 8.988 \times 10^{9}\ \frac{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}{\text{C}^2}\]

where:

\[\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\ \frac{\text{C}^2}{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}\]

The permittivity of free space characterizes how electric fields propagate through vacuum. We will see this constant appear again when discussing capacitors and electromagnetic waves.

*Personal note: The permittivity \(\varepsilon_0\) plays a role similar to \(G\) in gravity — it sets the “strength” of the interaction. But why \(4\pi\)? This factor appears naturally when considering spherical symmetry and will simplify Gauss’s Law in the next chapter.

Example: The Hydrogen Atom

The electron and proton of a hydrogen atom are separated (on average) by a distance of approximately \(r = 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\) m (the Bohr radius). Let’s compare the electric and gravitational forces between them.

Electric Force: \[F_E = k_e \frac{e^2}{r^2} = (8.988 \times 10^9) \frac{(1.602 \times 10^{-19})^2}{(5.3 \times 10^{-11})^2}\] \[F_E = 8.2 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{N}\]

Gravitational Force: \[F_g = G \frac{m_e m_p}{r^2} = (6.674 \times 10^{-11}) \frac{(9.109 \times 10^{-31})(1.673 \times 10^{-27})}{(5.3 \times 10^{-11})^2}\] \[F_g = 3.6 \times 10^{-47}\ \text{N}\]

Ratio: \[\frac{F_E}{F_g} = \frac{8.2 \times 10^{-8}}{3.6 \times 10^{-47}} \approx 2 \times 10^{39}\]

The electric force is about 10³⁹ times stronger than the gravitational force between these two particles. This is why we can completely ignore gravity when analyzing atomic and molecular interactions.

*Compare this to the \(10^{36}\) listed in the table back in §22.0 — the same ratio, apparently off by a thousand. Both are right. The table compares two protons; this example compares an electron and a proton. Swapping one proton for an electron divides the mass product by about 1,800 while leaving the charges untouched, and gravity weakens by exactly that factor. Whenever you see a “relative strength” quoted, ask what it is a comparison between — and notice that the conclusion survives regardless: whether the answer is \(10^{36}\) or \(10^{39}\), gravity is utterly negligible here. An order-of-magnitude conclusion this lopsided cannot be overturned by improving the precision of any input.

22.3 — The Electric Field

From Force to Field

In Physics I, we computed gravitational acceleration \(g\) by dividing the gravitational force by the test mass:

\[g = \frac{F_g}{m}\]

This gave us a quantity that depends only on the source of the field (Earth), not on the test object. We can do the same thing with electric force!

The electric field \(\vec{E}\) at a point in space is defined as the electric force per unit charge that would be experienced by a small positive test charge placed at that point:

\[\vec{E} = \frac{\vec{F}}{q_0}\]

where \(q_0\) is a small positive test charge.

Gravitational Analogy

Gravitational Electric
\(\vec{g} = \dfrac{\vec{F}_g}{m}\) \(\vec{E} = \dfrac{\vec{F}_E}{q}\)
Field due to source mass \(M\): \(g = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}\) Field due to source charge \(Q\): \(E = \dfrac{k_e Q}{r^2}\)
Force on test mass: \(\vec{F} = m\vec{g}\) Force on test charge: \(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\)
Units: m/s² (acceleration) Units: N/C or V/m

Just as gravitational acceleration exists everywhere around a massive object (whether or not a test mass is present), the electric field exists everywhere around a charged object (whether or not a test charge is present).

Electric Field Due to a Point Charge

For a single point charge \(Q\), the electric field at distance \(r\) is:

\[\vec{E} = k_e \frac{Q}{r^2} \hat{r}\]

where \(\hat{r}\) points radially outward from the charge.

Direction Convention:

  • For a positive source charge: \(\vec{E}\) points away from the charge
  • For a negative source charge: \(\vec{E}\) points toward the charge

The magnitude is: \[E = k_e \frac{|Q|}{r^2}\]

Force on a Charge in an Electric Field

Once we know the electric field at a point, we can find the force on any charge placed there:

\[\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\]

This is analogous to \(\vec{F} = m\vec{g}\) for gravity.

Direction of Force:

  • A positive charge experiences a force in the same direction as \(\vec{E}\)
  • A negative charge experiences a force opposite to \(\vec{E}\)

“Electrical Acceleration”

Combining \(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\) with Newton’s Second Law \(\vec{F} = m\vec{a}\):

\[\vec{a} = \frac{q\vec{E}}{m}\]

This is the acceleration of a charged particle in an electric field — analogous to \(\vec{a} = \vec{g}\) for a mass in a gravitational field.

For a uniform electric field (constant \(\vec{E}\)), this acceleration is constant, and we can use our familiar kinematic equations from Physics I!

22.4 — Electric Field from Multiple Charges

Superposition Principle

The electric field obeys the principle of superposition: the total electric field at any point is the vector sum of the electric fields due to all individual charges.

For \(N\) discrete point charges:

\[\vec{E} = k_e \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{q_i}{r_i^2} \hat{r}_i\]

This is just vector addition — the same technique we used for forces in Physics I!

Resultant Force on a Charge

If a charge \(q\) is in the presence of multiple other charges, the net force on it is the vector sum of all individual Coulomb forces:

\[\vec{F}_1 = \vec{F}_{21} + \vec{F}_{31} + \vec{F}_{41} + \cdots\]

where \(\vec{F}_{21}\) is the force on charge 1 due to charge 2, etc.

Example: Electric Field from Two Charges

Geometry (as in the figure): \(q_{1}\) sits a distance \(x_{1}\) to the left of the \(y\)-axis and \(q_{2}\) a distance \(x_{2}\) to the right, both on the \(x\)-axis, with the field point P at \((0,\ y)\). Let \(\theta\) be the angle \(\vec{E}_{1}\) makes with the horizontal and \(\phi\) the angle \(\vec{E}_{2}\) makes with it.

\[\vec{E} = \vec{E}_{1} + \vec{E}_{2}\]

\[\vec{E}_{1} = E_{1x}\widehat{i} + E_{1y}\widehat{j}, \qquad \vec{E}_{2} = E_{2x}\widehat{i} + E_{2y}\widehat{j}\]

Both charges are positive, so each field points away from its own source: \(\vec{E}_{1}\) up and to the right, \(\vec{E}_{2}\) up and to the left. That one reading of the picture fixes all four signs.

\[E_{1x} = E_{1}\cos\theta, \quad E_{1y} = E_{1}\sin\theta, \qquad E_{2x} = -E_{2}\cos\phi, \quad E_{2y} = E_{2}\sin\phi\]

\[\vec{E} = \left( E_{1}\cos\theta - E_{2}\cos\phi \right)\widehat{i} + \left( E_{1}\sin\theta + E_{2}\sin\phi \right)\widehat{j}\]

Now the magnitudes, \(E = k_{e}q/r^{2}\) taken one charge at a time:

\[\vec{E} = \left( \frac{k_{e}q_{1}}{r_{1}^{2}}\cos\theta - \frac{k_{e}q_{2}}{r_{2}^{2}}\cos\phi \right)\widehat{i} + \left( \frac{k_{e}q_{1}}{r_{1}^{2}}\sin\theta + \frac{k_{e}q_{2}}{r_{2}^{2}}\sin\phi \right)\widehat{j}\]

and then the angles — which are not independent information at all, but ratios of sides of triangles the coordinates already gave you:

\[\cos\theta = \frac{x_{1}}{r_{1}}, \quad \sin\theta = \frac{y}{r_{1}}, \qquad \cos\phi = \frac{x_{2}}{r_{2}}, \quad \sin\phi = \frac{y}{r_{2}}\]

\[\vec{E} = k_{e}\left[ \left( \frac{q_{1}x_{1}}{r_{1}^{3}} - \frac{q_{2}x_{2}}{r_{2}^{3}} \right)\widehat{i} + \left( \frac{q_{1}y}{r_{1}^{3}} + \frac{q_{2}y}{r_{2}^{3}} \right)\widehat{j} \right]\]

Watch what just happened to \(\theta\) and \(\phi\): they are gone. Substituting the ratios removed every trace of them, and what remains depends only on \(q_{1}\), \(q_{2}\), \(x_{1}\), \(x_{2}\) and \(y\) — the numbers the problem handed you. The angles were bookkeeping, never inputs. With \(r_{1} = \sqrt{x_{1}^{2} + y^{2}}\) and \(r_{2} = \sqrt{x_{2}^{2} + y^{2}}\):

\[\vec{E} = k_{e}\left[ \left( \frac{q_{1}x_{1}}{\left( x_{1}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}} - \frac{q_{2}x_{2}}{\left( x_{2}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}} \right)\widehat{i} + \left( \frac{q_{1}y}{\left( x_{1}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}} + \frac{q_{2}y}{\left( x_{2}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}} \right)\widehat{j} \right]\]

Place the charges symmetrically, \(x_{1} = x_{2} = x\), so that \(\theta = \phi\) and \(r_{1} = r_{2}\):

\[\boxed{\;\vec{E} = \frac{k_{e}}{\left( x^{2} + y^{2} \right)^{3/2}}\left[\, x\left( q_{1} - q_{2} \right)\widehat{i} + y\left( q_{1} + q_{2} \right)\widehat{j} \,\right]\;}\]

The \(\widehat{i}\) term is carried by the difference of the charges and the \(\widehat{j}\) term by their sum. Notice immediately what that means: if \(q_{2}\) is negative, the field stacks in \(x\) and cancels in \(y\) — the two behaviours trade places, and you can see it before computing anything.

\[q_{1} = q_{2} = q: \qquad \boxed{\;\vec{E} = \frac{2k_{e}q\, y}{\left( x^{2} + y^{2} \right)^{3/2}}\,\widehat{j}\;} \qquad \text{and for } y \gg x, \quad \vec{E} \approx \frac{k_{e}(2q)}{y^{2}}\,\widehat{j}\]

\[q_{1} = q,\ q_{2} = -q: \qquad \boxed{\;\vec{E} = \frac{2k_{e}q\, x}{\left( x^{2} + y^{2} \right)^{3/2}}\,\widehat{i}\;} \qquad \text{and for } y \gg x, \quad \vec{E} \approx \frac{2k_{e}q x}{y^{3}}\,\widehat{i}\]

Far away, the sum survives as \(1/y^{2}\) and is indistinguishable from a single charge \(2q\) — which is exactly what should happen. The difference survives as \(1/y^{3}\), faster than any point charge, because what is left is only the residue after a near-cancellation. Recognizing a vanishing component before computing anything is the most valuable habit in this chapter, and it is the same move that makes the continuous distributions in §22.5 tractable.

Magnitude and Direction

The components are the answer, but the answer is usually asked for as a size and a heading. Reserve a new symbol for that heading — \(\alpha\), measured from the \(+x\)-axis — because it is an output of the calculation, not one of the angles that went in.

\[E = \sqrt{E_{x}^{2} + E_{y}^{2}}, \qquad \tan\alpha = \frac{E_{y}}{E_{x}}\]

In full generality this is unlovely, but it is explicit and it is finished:

\[E = \sqrt{\left[ k_{e}\left( \frac{q_{1}x_{1}}{\left( x_{1}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}} - \frac{q_{2}x_{2}}{\left( x_{2}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}} \right) \right]^{2} + \left[ k_{e}\left( \frac{q_{1}y}{\left( x_{1}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}} + \frac{q_{2}y}{\left( x_{2}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}} \right) \right]^{2}}\]

\[\alpha = \arctan\left[ \frac{\dfrac{q_{1}y}{\left( x_{1}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}} + \dfrac{q_{2}y}{\left( x_{2}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}}}{\dfrac{q_{1}x_{1}}{\left( x_{1}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}} - \dfrac{q_{2}x_{2}}{\left( x_{2}^{2}+y^{2} \right)^{3/2}}} \right]\]

In the symmetric case the common factor comes out and the whole thing collapses:

\[E = \frac{k_{e}}{\left( x^{2} + y^{2} \right)^{3/2}}\sqrt{\left[ x\left( q_{1} - q_{2} \right) \right]^{2} + \left[ y\left( q_{1} + q_{2} \right) \right]^{2}}, \qquad \alpha = \arctan\left[ \frac{y}{x}\,\frac{q_{1} + q_{2}}{q_{1} - q_{2}} \right]\]

And now the direction of each limiting case falls out with no arithmetic at all:

\[q_{1} = q_{2} = q: \quad \alpha = \arctan\left[ \text{undefined} \right] = 90° \qquad\qquad q_{1} = q,\ q_{2} = -q: \quad \alpha = \arctan\left[ 0 \right] = 0°\]

Read those two against the pictures. Equal charges put P on a line of symmetry, so the field there can only point straight up the \(y\)-axis — \(\alpha = 90°\), and the arctangent tells you so by dividing by zero. Equal and opposite charges cancel the vertical entirely, leaving a field straight along \(x\) — \(\alpha = 0°\). Neither required evaluating a single number. The structure of the boxed result decided both.

Putting Numbers In

\(q_{1} = +4.00\) nC at \(x_{1} = -5.00\) cm and \(q_{2} = +2.00\) nC at \(x_{2} = +9.00\) cm, with P at \((0,\ 12.0)\) cm. The arrangement is not symmetric, so the general line applies rather than either boxed limit.

\[\vec{r}_{1} = 5.00\,\widehat{i} + 12.0\,\widehat{j}\ \text{cm}, \quad r_{1} = 13.0\ \text{cm} \qquad\qquad \vec{r}_{2} = -9.00\,\widehat{i} + 12.0\,\widehat{j}\ \text{cm}, \quad r_{2} = 15.0\ \text{cm}\]

\[\vec{E} = (16364)\left( 0.0500\,\widehat{i} + 0.120\,\widehat{j} \right) + (5326)\left( -0.0900\,\widehat{i} + 0.120\,\widehat{j} \right)\]

\[\vec{E} = \left( 818\,\widehat{i} + 1964\,\widehat{j} \right) + \left( -479\,\widehat{i} + 639\,\widehat{j} \right)\]

\[\boxed{\;\vec{E} = 339\,\widehat{i} + 2603\,\widehat{j}\ \ \text{N/C}, \qquad E = 2.62\times10^{3}\ \text{N/C}, \qquad \alpha = 82.6°\;}\]

The horizontal parts oppose and very nearly spend each other; the vertical parts add outright. That is the \(\left( q_{1} - q_{2} \right)\) and \(\left( q_{1} + q_{2} \right)\) structure of the boxed result showing up before the arrangement was made symmetric. Note also that \(\alpha\) is an output — the direction of the answer, measured from the \(+x\)-axis. No angle was supplied to get here.

The same geometry, one sign flipped. Let \(q_{2} = -2.00\) nC instead. Every distance is unchanged and both magnitudes are exactly what they were; only the second term changes sign, so \(\left( -479\,\widehat{i} + 639\,\widehat{j} \right)\) becomes \(\left( 479\,\widehat{i} - 639\,\widehat{j} \right)\).

\[\vec{E} = 1297\,\widehat{i} + 1325\,\widehat{j}\ \ \text{N/C}, \qquad E = 1.85\times10^{3}\ \text{N/C}, \qquad \alpha = 45.6°\]

Not one distance and not one magnitude changed, yet the answer swung from \(82.6°\) to \(45.6°\) and lost nearly a third of its size. Every bit of that came from direction alone, and the roles of the components swapped: the horizontal parts now add while the vertical parts oppose. The near-\(45°\) is a coincidence — \(E_x\) and \(E_y\) simply happen to land close together — and it disappears the moment either charge changes.

A Check: the Law of Cosines

\(\vec{E}_{1}\), \(\vec{E}_{2}\) and their sum form a triangle, so the magnitude can also be had from the law of cosines — provided you can name the angle it wants:

\[E^{2} = E_{1}^{2} + E_{2}^{2} - 2E_{1}E_{2}\cos\gamma\]

That angle is \(\gamma\) in Figure 22.5: the interior angle where \(\vec{E}_{2}\) is carried over tip-to-tail from the head of \(\vec{E}_{1}\). It is not a new quantity — it is the sum of the two angles the fields already make with the horizontal.

\[\gamma = \theta + \phi = 67.4° + 53.1° = 120.5°\]

\[E = \sqrt{\left( 2127 \right)^{2} + \left( 799 \right)^{2} - 2\left( 2127 \right)\left( 799 \right)\cos 120.5°} = 2.62 \times 10^{3}\ \text{N/C}\]

the same number the components gave. Note what it does not give you: the direction. \(\alpha\) still has to come from \(E_{x}\) and \(E_{y}\), or from a second application of the law of sines. That is the reason to learn the component route rather than this one — it finishes the problem in a single pass, and this does not.

The Electric Dipole

An electric dipole is the second boxed limit above: equal and opposite charges, \(+q\) and \(-q\), separated by \(2a\). It is worth its own name because it is the leading behaviour of any neutral object with separated charge — a water molecule, an antenna, a polarized atom.

Along the perpendicular bisector the field falls off as \(1/y^{3}\) rather than \(1/y^{2}\). A dipole is neutral, so from far enough away it must look like nothing at all; the \(1/y^{3}\) is how fast “nearly nothing” arrives.

22.5 — Electric Field from Continuous Charge Distributions (Calculus Extension)

From Discrete to Continuous

In the previous section, we considered discrete point charges. But what if charge is spread continuously over a line, surface, or volume?

We cannot simply sum over individual charges — instead, we must integrate.

The Integral Form

For a continuous charge distribution, the electric field is:

\[\vec{E} = k_e \int \frac{dq}{r^2} \hat{r}\]

where \(dq\) is an infinitesimal charge element at distance \(r\) from the field point.

Charge Density

The relationship between \(dq\) and the geometry depends on how the charge is distributed:

Linear charge density (charge per unit length): \[\lambda = \frac{dq}{dx} \quad \Rightarrow \quad dq = \lambda\, dx\] Units: C/m

Surface charge density (charge per unit area): \[\sigma = \frac{dq}{dA} \quad \Rightarrow \quad dq = \sigma\, dA\] Units: C/m²

Volume charge density (charge per unit volume): \[\rho = \frac{dq}{dV} \quad \Rightarrow \quad dq = \rho\, dV\] Units: C/m³

Example: Electric Field from a Semicircular Arc

A thin wire is bent into a semicircle of radius \(R\) carrying total charge \(Q\) spread uniformly along its length. Find the electric field at the center of the circle.

Put the arc in the upper half-plane with its centre at the origin, and let \(\theta\) measure position along it from the \(+x\)-axis. Let \(\lambda = Q/\pi R\).

\[\vec{E} = \int \frac{k_e\, dq}{R^{2}}\,\widehat{r}\]

\[dq = \lambda R\, d\theta\]

Every element sits the same distance \(R\) from the centre, so \(R\) never varies and comes straight out of the integral:

\[dE = \frac{k_e\, dq}{R^{2}} = \frac{k_e \lambda\, d\theta}{R}\]

Resist the temptation to declare a component zero on sight. Take one element, at angle \(\theta\), and write both of its components. The element sits at \(R\left( \cos\theta,\ \sin\theta \right)\), and for \(\lambda > 0\) the field it makes at the centre points away from it, along \(-\left( \cos\theta,\ \sin\theta \right)\):

\[d\vec{E} = -\frac{k_e\lambda\, d\theta}{R}\left( \cos\theta\, \widehat{i} + \sin\theta\, \widehat{j} \right)\]

\[E_x = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\int \cos\theta\, d\theta, \qquad\qquad E_y = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\int \sin\theta\, d\theta\]

Nothing has been thrown away and no symmetry has been claimed. The physics is finished; what remains is a question about limits. For the semicircle they run from \(0\) to \(\pi\):

\[E_x = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\Big[\sin\theta\Big]_{0}^{\pi} = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\left( 0 - 0 \right) = 0, \qquad E_y = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\Big[-\cos\theta\Big]_{0}^{\pi} = -\frac{2k_e\lambda}{R}\]

The zero was computed, not asserted. \(\sin\pi - \sin 0 = 0\) — that is the symmetry argument, performed by the integral rather than substituted for it. It is the same event as \(\left( q_{1} - q_{2} \right)\) vanishing in §22.4: write both components, then read which one the structure kills.

\[\boxed{\;\vec{E} = -\frac{2k_e\lambda}{R}\,\widehat{j}, \qquad E = \frac{2k_e\lambda}{R} = \frac{2k_e Q}{\pi R^2}\;}\]

directed along the arc’s axis of symmetry, away from the arc for positive \(Q\).

Is that reasonable? Collapse the same charge \(Q\) into a single point at the same distance \(R\) and you would get \(k_eQ/R^2\). The arc delivers \(2/\pi \approx 64\%\) of that. Spreading charge out always costs you field strength relative to concentrating it at the same distance — the off-axis parts of each contribution cancel against each other and are simply lost. That ratio, \(2/\pi\), is the price of the spreading.

Change One Limit: the Quarter Arc

Nothing in the setup above was special to a half-circle. Bend the same wire into a quarter in the first quadrant, keeping \(\lambda\) and \(R\), and every line up to the integrals is unchanged. Only the upper limit moves, from \(\pi\) to \(\pi/2\):

\[E_x = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\Big[\sin\theta\Big]_{0}^{\pi/2} = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\left( 1 - 0 \right) = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\]

\[E_y = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\Big[-\cos\theta\Big]_{0}^{\pi/2} = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\left( 0 + 1 \right) = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\]

\[\boxed{\;\vec{E} = -\frac{k_e\lambda}{R}\left( \widehat{i} + \widehat{j} \right), \qquad E = \frac{\sqrt{2}\,k_e\lambda}{R}\;}\]

directed at \(45°\) below the \(-x\) axis. This time nothing vanished. The same cosine integral that returned zero across a full half-turn returns \(1\) across a quarter, so both components survive — and the quarter arc’s field is not along either axis.

Why are the two components equal? Because the quarter arc is symmetric about the \(45°\) line, so it cannot prefer \(x\) over \(y\). Notice what that symmetry did and did not do: it predicted that the two answers would match, which is a useful check, but it removed no work. Compare that with the half-circle, where the symmetry genuinely killed an integral. Symmetry is a gift when you get one; it is not a method.

One Formula for Any Arc

Both results above are cases of a single statement. Put \(\theta\) on the arc’s own axis of symmetry rather than the \(x\)-axis, letting it run from \(-\theta_{0}\) to \(+\theta_{0}\), so the arc has opening angle \(2\theta_{0}\). The perpendicular component then vanishes for every arc at once — its integrand is odd and the limits are symmetric — and with total charge \(Q = 2\lambda R\theta_{0}\) the survivor is

\[\boxed{\;E = \frac{k_e Q}{R^{2}} \cdot \frac{\sin\theta_{0}}{\theta_{0}}\;}\]

Shrink the arc and watch Coulomb’s law come back. As \(\theta_{0} \rightarrow 0\) the charge \(Q\) crowds onto a single point at distance \(R\), and \(\sin\theta_{0}/\theta_{0} \rightarrow 1\), leaving \(E \rightarrow k_{e}Q/R^{2}\). The integral did not replace Coulomb’s law — it generalised it, and this is the proof. The whole factor \(\sin\theta_{0}/\theta_{0}\) is the price of spreading: exactly \(1\) for a point, and falling as the charge is smeared around the circle. At \(\theta_{0} = \pi/2\) it is \(2/\pi\), which is the \(64\%\) found above; at \(\theta_{0} = \pi\) the arc closes into a full ring, \(\sin\pi = 0\), and the field at the centre is zero — as it must be.

*Notice what actually did the work here. Not the integral — that was one line. It was writing both components before deciding anything, which let the limits report which one survives instead of you guessing. Every continuous distribution you will meet, whether a rod, a ring, a disk, or an infinite sheet, is the same five moves: choose \(dq\), write \(r\), write both components, integrate, then check a limit. Chapter 23 promotes this instinct to a law.

22.6 — Electric Field Lines

Visualizing the Electric Field

Electric field lines are a powerful tool for visualizing electric fields. They were introduced by Michael Faraday, who called them “lines of force.”

Rules for Drawing Electric Field Lines:

  1. Direction: Field lines point in the direction of the electric field at each point. A small positive test charge would accelerate in the direction of the field line.

  2. Origin and Termination: Field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges (or extend to infinity).

  3. Density = Strength: The number of lines per unit area perpendicular to the lines is proportional to the field strength. Closely spaced lines indicate a strong field.

  4. No Crossing: Electric field lines never cross. At each point in space, there is a unique field direction.

  5. Perpendicular to Conductors: Field lines meet conducting surfaces at right angles.

Field Line Patterns

Single Positive Charge: Lines radiate outward uniformly in all directions (like a “starburst”).

Single Negative Charge: Lines point radially inward (the opposite pattern).

Electric Dipole: Lines curve from the positive charge to the negative charge, forming characteristic looping patterns.

Two Like Charges: Lines repel each other, curving away. There is a point between the charges where the field is zero.

Uniform Field (Parallel Plates): Between two large parallel plates with opposite charges, field lines are straight, parallel, and evenly spaced.

Field Lines and Flux

The density of field lines (number of lines per unit area) is proportional to the electric field magnitude. This concept will be formalized as electric flux in Chapter 23 when we introduce Gauss’s Law.

Equipotentials: What the Lab Actually Measures

In lab (Experiment 203, Electric Field Mapping) you will not measure field lines. A voltmeter probe reads electric potential, so what you can actually map are the curves along which that reading does not change. These are called equipotentials: surfaces on which no work is required to move a charge from one point to another.

The two pictures are linked by a single geometric fact:

Equipotentials always cross electric field lines at right angles.

That is what makes the experiment work. You map the equipotentials, draw the perpendiculars, and you have recovered the field lines you could not measure directly.

Rule 5 above is this same statement in disguise. The surface of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential — every point on it sits at the same potential — which is exactly why field lines must meet it square.

We are not defining potential yet; that is Chapter 24. For now, the word and the perpendicularity are enough to make sense of what appears on your plotting paper.

22.7 — Motion of a Charged Particle in a Uniform Electric Field

Projectile Motion Analogy

In Physics I, we studied projectile motion — an object moving under constant gravitational acceleration. The motion could be decomposed into independent horizontal and vertical components.

A charged particle in a uniform electric field behaves similarly! The constant field produces a constant acceleration:

\[\vec{a} = \frac{q\vec{E}}{m}\]

If the field points in one direction (say, \(+y\)), we can analyze the motion using our familiar kinematic equations:

Constant Acceleration Kinematics: \[v_f = v_i + at\] \[x_f = x_i + v_i t + \frac{1}{2}at^2\] \[v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2a(x_f - x_i)\]

Example: Proton in a Uniform Field

A proton moves at \(v_i = 4.50 \times 10^5\) m/s in the horizontal direction. It enters a uniform vertical electric field with magnitude \(E = 9.60 \times 10^3\) N/C directed upward. Ignoring gravity:

(A) Find the time for the proton to travel 5.00 cm horizontally.

The horizontal motion is unaffected by the vertical field: \[t = \frac{\Delta x}{v_x} = \frac{0.0500\ \text{m}}{4.50 \times 10^5\ \text{m/s}} = 1.11 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{s} = 111\ \text{ns}\]

(B) Find the vertical displacement during this time.

First, find the vertical acceleration: \[a_y = \frac{qE}{m_p} = \frac{(1.602 \times 10^{-19})(9.60 \times 10^3)}{1.673 \times 10^{-27}} = 9.19 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m/s}^2\]

Then: \[y_f = \frac{1}{2}a_y t^2 = \frac{1}{2}(9.19 \times 10^{11})(1.11 \times 10^{-7})^2 = 5.68 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 5.68\ \text{mm}\]

(C) Find the velocity components after traveling 5.00 cm horizontally.

\[v_x = 4.50 \times 10^5\ \text{m/s}\] (unchanged)

\[v_y = a_y t = (9.19 \times 10^{11})(1.11 \times 10^{-7}) = 1.02 \times 10^5\ \text{m/s}\]

\[\vec{v} = \left( 4.50 \times 10^5\ \widehat{i} + 1.02 \times 10^5\ \widehat{j} \right)\ \text{m/s}\]

Energy Considerations

We can also analyze motion using energy methods. The work done by the electric field on a charge is:

\[W = qE\Delta s = \Delta KE\]

This is analogous to \(W = mg\Delta h\) for gravitational work. The electric field does work on charges, converting electric potential energy to kinetic energy (or vice versa).

*We will develop this energy approach fully in Chapter 24 when we introduce Electric Potential.

22.8 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter. It is conserved and quantized in units of the elementary charge \(e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\) C.

  2. Coulomb’s Law describes the force between point charges: \[F = k_e \frac{|q_1||q_2|}{r^2}\]

  3. The electric field is force per unit charge: \[\vec{E} = \frac{\vec{F}}{q} = k_e \frac{Q}{r^2}\hat{r}\]

  4. The superposition principle allows us to find fields from multiple charges by vector addition.

  5. Electric field lines visualize the field: they begin on positive charges, end on negative charges, and their density indicates field strength.

  6. Charged particles in uniform fields undergo constant acceleration, analogous to projectile motion.

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Elementary charge \(e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\) C
Coulomb’s Law \(\vec{F} = k_e \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\hat{r}\)
Coulomb’s constant \(k_e = 8.988 \times 10^9\ \dfrac{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}{\text{C}^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\)
Permittivity of free space \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\ \dfrac{\text{C}^2}{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}\)
Electric field (point charge) \(\vec{E} = k_e \dfrac{Q}{r^2}\hat{r}\)
Force on charge in field \(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\)
Superposition (discrete) \(\vec{E} = k_e \sum_i \dfrac{q_i}{r_i^2}\hat{r}_i\)
Superposition (continuous) \(\vec{E} = k_e \int \dfrac{dq}{r^2}\hat{r}\)
Acceleration in field \(\vec{a} = \dfrac{q\vec{E}}{m}\)

Connections to Physics I

Mechanics Concept Electrostatics Analog
Mass (\(m\)) Charge (\(q\))
Gravitational constant (\(G\)) Coulomb’s constant (\(k_e\))
Gravitational field (\(\vec{g}\)) Electric field (\(\vec{E}\))
Weight (\(\vec{F} = m\vec{g}\)) Electric force (\(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\))
Free-fall acceleration Acceleration in uniform \(\vec{E}\)
Projectile motion Charged particle in uniform \(\vec{E}\)

Looking Ahead

In Chapter 23, we will introduce Gauss’s Law, a powerful tool for calculating electric fields using symmetry. This will greatly simplify problems involving continuous charge distributions and lead us toward understanding conductors and insulators in electrostatic equilibrium.

*One last thing worth carrying forward. Every result in this chapter rests on treating charges as points — objects with a position but no size. That idealization is what makes \(1/r^2\) meaningful, and it is also the first thing to break: at \(r \to 0\) the field diverges, which is physics telling you the model has left its domain, not that the field is infinite. Notice that our own hydrogen example sat at \(r = 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\) m — a distance defined by the electron’s orbit, which a point particle would not have. The model was already straining at the very scale where we used it, and it still gave the right answer to within a factor that did not matter. Knowing which idealization you are standing on, and where it gives way, is a larger part of physics than any single equation in this chapter.
